clue.text: Land in Siberia, part of journey being discussed

indicators.note: something being discussed is spoken about, so the word for the journey part is heard rather than seen

parts.note: a step is one stage or stride of a journey

explanation.surface: A traveller's account of a trek across Siberia, with one stage of the trip under discussion.
explanation.definitionFit: The vast treeless grasslands of Siberia and Central Asia are the classic example of such plains.

clue.text: Thunderstorm's beginning, cling to hood

indicators.note: the beginning of the word Thunderstorm is its opening letter

parts.note: to hug something is to cling to it tightly

explanation.surface: As a storm starts, someone pulls their hood close.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hood' looks like a garment, but here it is short for hoodlum.
explanation.definitionFit: A hood, short for hoodlum, is a violent criminal or gangster, a synonym.

clue.text: Officer's faithful colleague decorated in unlimited expression of remorse

indicators.note: one piece is placed in the other, so the frosted word goes inside the trimmed apology
without its limits, the word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: an apology expresses remorse
a cake decorated with icing is iced

explanation.surface: A decorated officer's loyal partner is honoured during a remorseful apology.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unlimited' trims the outer letters of the remorseful word, and 'in' sets the decorating word inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A trained canine working alongside constables is a policeman's loyal partner.

clue.text: Range that's 20 in film

indicators.note: the number goes in the film, sitting between its two letters

parts.note: E.T. is Spielberg's 1982 film about an extra-terrestrial
X is the Roman numeral ten, and TEN is ten again: ten plus ten makes twenty

explanation.surface: A film's range is twenty, as if quoting a rating.
explanation.walkthrough: '20' is not a cross-reference here: it is written as X plus TEN, two tens.
explanation.definitionFit: Range and this word both mean the scope or area something covers.

clue.text: Supporter covering grass for sporting occasion

indicators.note: the support piece covers the grass word, holding it inside

parts.note: a brace is a support or prop
the oat is a cereal grass

explanation.surface: A stand covering a grass pitch for a big sporting event.
explanation.walkthrough: The Boat Race is the annual Oxford v Cambridge rowing race on the Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: The annual university rowing contest is a famous British sporting event.

clue.text: Defensive attitude that may once have got Tiger Woods out of trouble?

definitions.meaning: a siege mindset, believing oneself under attack and refusing to budge

definitions.text: may once have got Tiger Woods out of trouble?
definitions.meaning: read literally, the mental approach a golfer takes when stuck in a sand trap

explanation.surface: A golfer's defensive mindset rescuing Tiger Woods from a tight spot.
explanation.walkthrough: A bunker is a sand trap on a golf course; a golfer must think their way out of one.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a siege mindset of hunkering down against a hostile world.

clue.text: One doubts a jerk will keep number up

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so the jerk holds the number

parts.note: a tic is an involuntary jerk

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read bottom to top

parts.note: a song is a musical number

explanation.surface: A sceptic doubts that some idiot will keep their number up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses the number in this down clue, and 'will keep' places it inside the jerk.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who doubts whether God exists, holding that it cannot be known.

clue.text: Brief stop

definitions.meaning: as a noun, the terms of reference or task given to someone
as a verb, to cease or desist, as in easing off an effort

explanation.definitionFit: The noun is a task assignment; the verb can mean to slacken or cease.

clue.text: In fitful pain, wine not finished: I'm surprised! One's always at the bar!

indicators.note: the wine and exclamation go in the pain word, after its first letter

parts.note: colic is pain that comes in fits or spasms

indicators.note: without its finish, the wine loses its last letter

parts.note: hock is German white wine
oh is an exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: A drunk in spasms of pain at the pub, cradling unfinished wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not finished' cuts HOCK to HOC; the bar is a chocolate bar, not a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone addicted to chocolate is always reaching for a bar of the stuff.

clue.text: Announcement: target has been hit?

definitions.meaning: read as two words, a bullet is in, which is what happens when a target is hit

explanation.surface: A news flash reports that the target has been struck.
explanation.definitionFit: A short news report or official statement issued to the public.

clue.text: Hunter put game on stick

indicators.note: one piece is put on the other, so the game comes before the stick

parts.note: Nim is a game of taking objects from heaps
a rod is a stick

explanation.surface: A hunter puts his quarry on a stick to carry it home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game' looks like the hunter's quarry; it is the game Nim.
explanation.definitionFit: Nimrod is the mighty hunter of Genesis, whose name came to mean any hunter.

clue.text: In which babbling voices rant on?

definitions.text: In which babbling voices rant on?

indicators.note: babbling speech is confused and jumbled, so these letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A description of a talk in which voices babble and rant on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'babbling' rearranges the letters of VOICES RANT ON, and the whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A talk between people is where voices go on, sometimes babbling and ranting.

clue.text: Partner of footballer always tackling scorer, one has a job

parts.note: WAG is British tabloid slang for a footballer's wife or girlfriend

indicators.note: to tackle is to take hold of, so the word for always grips the composer

parts.note: e'er is the poetic short form of ever, meaning always
Thomas Arne, composer of Rule Britannia, wrote musical scores

explanation.surface: A footballer's partner keeps tackling the player who scores.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scorer' looks like a goal-getter, but it means a composer, held by 'tackling' inside the poetic form of ever.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyone paid wages for work is someone with a job, a definition by description.

clue.text: See 23
Round of leaflets ending in porch and I almost exploded!

indicators.note: something exploded is blown apart, so these letters are scattered into a new order
the ending of the word porch is its final letter

explanation.surface: Junk mail piles up in the porch and the householder almost loses their temper.
explanation.definitionFit: A mass mailing of advertising leaflets, sent out in one batch.

clue.text: Remarkable bird circling peak in Tibet

indicators.note: the bird goes round the letter, enclosing it

parts.note: the starling is a common songbird

indicators.note: the peak of a word in a down clue is its top, first letter

explanation.surface: A rare bird circling a Himalayan summit.
explanation.definitionFit: Startling and remarkable both describe something surprising enough to be noticed.

clue.text: Chaser possibly? I'm not sure one's a hunter

indicators.note: possibly signals another possible arrangement of these letters

parts.note: er is a hesitant sound of uncertainty

explanation.surface: Is a chaser perhaps a kind of hunter? The speaker hesitates.
explanation.definitionFit: A searcher hunts for something, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Colour to match in gaol

indicators.note: the matching word goes in the prison word, after its second letter

parts.note: pen is slang for a prison, short for penitentiary
to agree is to match or correspond

explanation.surface: Choosing a paint shade to match the walls of a prison.
explanation.definitionFit: A pale, bright yellowish shade of green, a specific named hue.

clue.text: A figure turns — on this?

indicators.note: a word that turns is read the other way round

parts.note: six is a figure, a number

explanation.surface: Asks what a spinning figure rotates about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' reverses the figure, and the whole clue doubles as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Any rotating body spins about a central line, which is exactly what this word names.

clue.text: Thick sauce and pieces of meat, but no starter served up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the pieces are read bottom to top

parts.note: a dip is a thick sauce for dunking

indicators.note: with no starter, the word loses its first letter

parts.note: cuts are pieces of meat from a butcher

explanation.surface: A thick sauce and cuts of meat served without a first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thick' looks like a description of the sauce, but it is the definition. 'no starter' turns CUTS into UTS; DIPUTS read upwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Thick, as an insult, means slow-witted or dim, a synonym.

clue.text: Knock back and forth

definitions.note: James Joyce's word in Ulysses imitating the rapping of a knock at the door

indicators.note: the word reads the same back and forth, so the letters form a palindrome

parts.note: James Joyce's word in Ulysses imitating the rapping of a knock at the door

explanation.surface: Someone raps on a door, then knocks some more, this way and that.
explanation.walkthrough: James Joyce coined this word in Ulysses for a knock on the door; it is the longest palindrome in the OED.
explanation.definitionFit: Joyce's coinage imitates the rapping sound of a knock at the door, and is spelt identically either way.

clue.text: Strike head of teddy bear

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: in British usage, to hump something is to carry or bear it

explanation.surface: Someone hits a teddy bear on the head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bear' looks like the toy, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To thump is to strike heavily, as with a fist.

clue.text: Battle in Belgium on Sunday

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of words, across their boundaries

explanation.surface: A battle was fought in Belgium on a Sunday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Battle in Belgium' looks like the definition; only 'Battle' is, and the town is actually in Belgium too.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1914 Battle of Mons was the British Army's first major action of the First World War.

clue.text: Scrabble has no guide, no further explanation required

indicators.note: to scrabble is to scramble or scratch about, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A Scrabble player without a rule book needs no more explaining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrabble' looks like the board game; it is a verb meaning scramble.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is said when a matter is clear and nothing more need be said.

clue.text: Lock up the little devil, having rejected classroom show of dissent?

parts.note: an imp is a little devil

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the phrase is read backwards

parts.note: a pupil refusing a teacher might say no, sir

explanation.surface: A teacher wants to lock up an unruly pupil who answers back.
explanation.definitionFit: To lock someone up is to jail them, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Possessions for forward delivery, ultimately

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
pert means cheeky or forward

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so the last letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: Belongings to be sent by advance delivery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forward delivery' reads as one shipping term; the words split.
explanation.definitionFit: What someone owns is their property, a collective synonym for possessions.

clue.text: Summary, like one this short, ends

parts.note: to dig something is slang for liking it

indicators.note: the ends of the three words are their final letters

explanation.surface: A summary as brief as this one, with nothing more to add.
explanation.definitionFit: A digest is a condensed summary of a longer text or body of news.
